study.title: Ezekiel 46 - Order of worship, prince's limits and temple kitchens
study.overview: Ezekiel 46 describes, with a strong sense of order and reverence, how restored worship should work in the temple: the eastern door, once closed, opens at specific times; the prince participates as representative of the people, but without exceeding the place that fits him; and the temple receives own spaces for the preparation of the offerings. The chapter unites liturgy, authority and holiness. He shows that worship of the Lord is not improvised, but regulated by God, and that even civil government must submit to the worship of the Lord. At the same time, the text preserves distinctions: the people worship, the priests mediate, the prince leads, and each function has clear limits.

outline.title: Rules for the Sabbath, the new moon and the daily sacrifices
outline.explanation: The eastern door of the inner courtyard opens on specific holy days. The prince enters a certain path, worships in a limited place and offers sacrifices in the name of the people. The people also participate, but without unrestricted access to the interior. The text sets standards for burnt offerings, cereal and olive oil offerings, both in monthly and weekly celebrations and daily, reinforcing the continuity of the cult.

outline.title: Limits for the Prince's Heritage
outline.explanation: The prince may transfer part of his inheritance to his children, but he must not take away the inheritance of the people to favor anyone. To donate to servants, possession is temporary until the year of freedom. The rule protects the stability of the people and prevents abuse of power, showing that the authority of the prince is real, but not absolute.

outline.title: Chambers of priests and kitchens of offerings
outline.explanation: The prophet is brought to the reserved dependencies on the priests, where sacrifices for sin and guilt would be prepared. Then you see the four corners of the outside courtyard, with enclosed patios and kitchens around the walls. These spaces serve to cook the offerings of the people, indicating a practical organization for worship and preserving the holiness of the sacred space.

study.context: The chapter is part of the final vision of the temple in Ezekiel 40-46. The text itself shows a guided tour of the temple, with attention to doors, courtyards, cameras and places of preparation of the offerings. The scenario presupposes an order of restored worship, in which priests, prince and people have defined functions. It is not possible to affirm, based only on this chapter and the notes given, whether these instructions were observed literally at some later historical phase; Matthew Henry's notes observe this uncertainty. The focus of the text is on the sanctity of worship and in the discipline of community life before God.
study.theology: The chapter presents a theology of holiness that organizes even the most concrete details of worship. God determines when the door opens, who can enter, how the sacrifice is offered and where it should be prepared. This teaches that true worship is not the product of the human will, but an obedient response to divine revelation. The prince appears as a representative of the people, which suggests leadership subordinated to God, not political autonomy. Priestly mediation is also maintained: even the prince does not place himself directly at the center of the sacred. In addition, the protection of the people's inheritance denounces economic injustice and prevents abusive concentration of land. Finally, the kitchens show that communion with God also includes concrete provision, sharing and correct use of temple resources; the offering is not only rite, but food and communion ordered before the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The eastern door would be opened on the Sabbath, on the new moon and when the prince willingly offered burnt offerings or peaceful offerings; this highlights the role of the prince as a representative worshiper of the people.
The law limits the power of the prince in the distribution of his inheritance, so that he does not use the position to impoverish the people or to disorder the possession of the lands.
The kitchens served to prepare the parts of the peaceful offerings that would be devour food, and the practical purpose also included sustaining sharing and mercy.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to worship God with the reverence and order that the chapter requires?
In what ways can a leader serve as a representative of the people without taking for themselves what belongs to him?
How does this chapter correct the tendency to separate God worship of justice, sharing and community responsibility?
study.practice: Take the order of worship and the integrity of leadership seriously. This chapter invites the church to plan worship with reverence, to recognize that all human authority is subordinate to the Lord and to protect the weakest from abuse. In practice, this can mean valuing well-prepared liturgy, server leadership, transparency in the use of resources and space for communion with God to produce concrete care for people.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow us to state whether the instructions were applied literally in some later historical period; this remains uncertain. It is also not possible to safely determine, only from this chapter and notes, all the architectural and functional details of the mentioned structures. The study seeks to follow the text and notes without dealing with confessional interpretations as indisputable conclusions.
